claim: GCaMP6f signals in apical tuft dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons are highly correlated (Pearson's correlation coefficient r = 0.92, SEM = 0.01, n = 25 fields of view recorded from 14 neurons, 6 animals).
source: Our results showed highly correlated calcium signals in all apical dendritic branches belonging to the same neuron and imaged in a given field of view (Pearson's correlation coefficient r = 0.92, SEM = 0.01, n = 25 fields of view recorded from 14 neurons, 6 animals) (Figure 1B, C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging measurements, as indicated by the specific statistical values and sample sizes provided.

claim: Calcium signals in sibling branches of apical tuft dendrites are highly correlated (average Pearson's correlation coefficient r = 0.92) regardless of their branching order.
source: We found that calcium signals in sibling branches were highly correlated (average Pearson's correlation coefficient r = 0.92) regardless of their branching order (One-way ANOVA, p=0.34) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation values across different branching orders with statistical testing (One-way ANOVA).

claim: Visual stimulation significantly increases mean ΔF/F0 of apical tuft dendrites (p=0.005).
source: Both visual stimulation and locomotion significantly increase the mean ΔF/F0 of tuft branches without any interaction effect (Repeated Measures Two-way ANOVA on log-transformed data, p=0.005, 0.003 and 0.99 for stim, loco and interaction effects respectively, mean (normalised to condition stim/still)=1; 2.15; 0.7; 1.4, sem = 0; 0.38; 0.08 and 0.3, n = 14 neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging during visual stimulation, with statistical analysis (Repeated Measures Two-way ANOVA).

claim: Locomotion significantly increases mean ΔF/F0 of apical tuft dendrites (p=0.003).
source: Both visual stimulation and locomotion significantly increase the mean ΔF/F0 of tuft branches without any interaction effect (Repeated Measures Two-way ANOVA on log-transformed data, p=0.005, 0.003 and 0.99 for stim, loco and interaction effects respectively, mean (normalised to condition stim/still)=1; 2.15; 0.7; 1.4, sem = 0; 0.38; 0.08 and 0.3, n = 14 neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging during locomotion periods, with statistical analysis.

claim: Branch-specific calcium transients in apical tuft dendrites represent less than 3% of the total number of transients.
source: Among the 70 imaged branches across 14 neurons, branch-specific calcium transients represented less than 3% of the total number of transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium transients across multiple branches and neurons.

claim: Branch-specific calcium signals are dominated by calcium transients of the smallest amplitudes.
source: Among all imaged calcium transients, these local signals were dominated by calcium transients of the smallest amplitudes (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by amplitude analysis of calcium transients shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Neither visual stimulation nor locomotion significantly affects the proportion of branch-specific calcium signals (Three-way ANOVA, p=0.29; 0.8 and 0.94, for visual stimulation, locomotion and interaction between both conditions, respectively).
source: In addition, neither visual stimulation nor locomotion significantly affected this small proportion of branch-specific calcium signals (Three-way ANOVA, p<10−15 for event amplitude and p=0.29; 0.8 and 0.94, for visual stimulation, locomotion and interaction between both conditions, respectively; no other interaction effect was statistically significant) (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Three-way ANOVA) of calcium transients under different behavioral and sensory conditions.

claim: The average Pearson's correlation value between peak amplitudes of calcium transients is 0.88 between proximal and distal parts of the apical tuft.
source: For each pair of compartments, we found that the average Pearson's correlation value between the peak amplitude of individual transients was 0.88 between the proximal and distal parts of the apical tuft, 0.92 between the trunk and the apical tuft and 0.85 between the proximal and distal trunk (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from semi-simultaneous two-plane imaging of different neuronal compartments.

claim: The average Pearson's correlation value between peak amplitudes of calcium transients is 0.92 between the trunk and the apical tuft.
source: For each pair of compartments, we found that the average Pearson's correlation value between the peak amplitude of individual transients was 0.88 between the proximal and distal parts of the apical tuft, 0.92 between the trunk and the apical tuft and 0.85 between the proximal and distal trunk (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from semi-simultaneous two-plane imaging.

claim: The average Pearson's correlation value between peak amplitudes of calcium transients is 0.85 between the proximal and distal trunk.
source: For each pair of compartments, we found that the average Pearson's correlation value between the peak amplitude of individual transients was 0.88 between the proximal and distal parts of the apical tuft, 0.92 between the trunk and the apical tuft and 0.85 between the proximal and distal trunk (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from semi-simultaneous two-plane imaging.

claim: The lowest correlation value (0.74) was found between the soma and the proximal trunk.
source: The lowest correlation value was found between the soma and the proximal trunk (0.74, Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from semi-simultaneous imaging of soma and trunk compartments.

claim: On average, 60% of events detected as branch-specific in apical tuft dendrites were also found in the trunk.
source: On average, we found that 60% of the events detected as branch-specific were also found in the trunk (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of calcium transients detected in both tuft branches and trunk compartments.

claim: The frequency of calcium transients decreases from proximal to distal compartments by an average of 14% from soma to proximal trunk.
source: We found that the frequency of calcium transients decreased from proximal to distal compartments (Paired t-test, p=1.1e−6, n = 31 pairs of compartments from 19 neurons) by an average of 14% from soma to proximal trunk, 8% from proximal to distal trunk, 24% from distal trunk to apical tuft and 22% from proximal tuft to distal tuft (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium transient frequencies across neuronal compartments with statistical testing.

claim: The frequency of calcium transients decreases from proximal to distal compartments by an average of 8% from proximal to distal trunk.
source: We found that the frequency of calcium transients decreased from proximal to distal compartments (Paired t-test, p=1.1e−6, n = 31 pairs of compartments from 19 neurons) by an average of 14% from soma to proximal trunk, 8% from proximal to distal trunk, 24% from distal trunk to apical tuft and 22% from proximal tuft to distal tuft (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium transient frequencies with statistical testing.

claim: The frequency of calcium transients decreases from proximal to distal compartments by an average of 24% from distal trunk to apical tuft.
source: We found that the frequency of calcium transients decreased from proximal to distal compartments (Paired t-test, p=1.1e−6, n = 31 pairs of compartments from 19 neurons) by an average of 14% from soma to proximal trunk, 8% from proximal to distal trunk, 24% from distal trunk to apical tuft and 22% from proximal tuft to distal tuft (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium transient frequencies with statistical testing.

claim: The frequency of calcium transients decreases from proximal to distal compartments by an average of 22% from proximal tuft to distal tuft.
source: We found that the frequency of calcium transients decreased from proximal to distal compartments (Paired t-test, p=1.1e−6, n = 31 pairs of compartments from 19 neurons) by an average of 14% from soma to proximal trunk, 8% from proximal to distal trunk, 24% from distal trunk to apical tuft and 22% from proximal tuft to distal tuft (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium transient frequencies with statistical testing.

claim: There is an estimated decrease of about 40% of calcium transients from soma to the distal part of the apical tuft.
source: From these proportions, we estimated a decrease of about 40% of calcium transients from soma to the distal part of the apical tuft (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations derived from measured decreases across compartment pairs.

claim: The mean frequency of calcium transients in the apical tuft corresponds to 62% of the frequency of events in the corresponding soma (n = 13 neurons).
source: We found that the mean frequency of calcium transients in the apical tuft corresponded to 62% of the frequency of events in the corresponding soma (n = 13 neurons Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by independent imaging data of soma and apical tuft compartments.

claim: Smaller amplitude calcium transients in the proximal compartment are more likely to attenuate below detection level in the distal compartment compared to larger amplitude events.
source: Our results show that smaller amplitude calcium transients in the proximal compartment were more likely to attenuate below detection level in the distal compartment compared to larger amplitudes events (red trace in Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by amplitude-dependent analysis of calcium transient attenuation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The vast majority of compartment-specific events are dominated by calcium transients in proximal compartments that are not detected in distal ones.
source: The vast majority of compartment-specific events were dominated by calcium transients in proximal compartments that were not detected in distal ones (red trace in Figure 3C), while only few calcium transients were found in distal compartments and not in the corresponding proximal compartment (blue trace in Figure 3C) (see also Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C and visual evidence in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: GCaMP6s can robustly detect somatic calcium signals with firing frequencies as low as 5 Hz.
source: For somatic stimulation, we found that we could robustly detect somatic calcium signals with firing frequencies as low as 5 Hz with GCaMP6s (Figure 4E, G), and as low as 25 Hz with GCaMP6f (Figure 4F, H)
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data combining calcium imaging and whole-cell recordings.

claim: GCaMP6f can robustly detect somatic calcium signals with firing frequencies as low as 25 Hz.
source: For somatic stimulation, we found that we could robustly detect somatic calcium signals with firing frequencies as low as 5 Hz with GCaMP6s (Figure 4E, G), and as low as 25 Hz with GCaMP6f (Figure 4F, H)
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data combining calcium imaging and whole-cell recordings.

claim: Single action potentials cannot be reliably detected with either GCaMP6s or GCaMP6f in layer 5 neurons ex vivo.
source: we could not reliably detect calcium events associated with single action potentials with either indicator (ΔF/F0 peak for GCaMP6s: mean = 0.02, sem = 0.01, t-test vs null, p=0.07, n = 10 neurons; ΔF/F0 peak for GCaMP6f: mean = −0.02, sem = 0.03, t-test vs null, p=0.39, n = 9 neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data with statistical testing showing no significant detection of single action potentials.

claim: In distal dendrites, reliable calcium signals for both GCaMP6s and GCaMP6f are only detected when somatically-driven spiking exceeds 50 Hz.
source: By contrast, in the distal dendrites, reliable signals for both indicators were only detected when somatically-driven spiking exceeded 50 Hz (Figure 4E–H), likely reflecting the critical frequency (50–100 Hz) of back-propagating action potentials required to trigger distal dendritic calcium spikes (Larkum et al., 1999a; Shai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data and is consistent with cited literature on back-propagating action potentials.

claim: Somatically-triggered back-propagating action potentials below the critical frequency (<50–100 Hz) may underlie the distance-dependent loss of dendritic calcium signals observed in vivo.
source: Our findings suggest that: 1) somatically-triggered back-propagating action potentials below the critical frequency (<50–100 Hz) may underlie the distant-dependent loss of dendritic calcium signals we observed in vivo
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ex vivo experimental findings and their interpretation in the context of in vivo observations.

claim: Spiking driven by strong apical tuft input or high-frequency spiking driven by somatic depolarization may underlie the strong somato-dendritic coupling detected in vivo.
source: 2) spiking driven by strong apical tuft input or high-frequency spiking driven by somatic depolarization may underlie the strong somato-dendritic coupling detected in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ex vivo experimental findings and their interpretation in the context of in vivo observations.

claim: Compared to GCaMP6s, GCaMP6f has a reduced sensitivity for detecting calcium signals, specifically in the soma during low frequency spiking driven either by somatic or dendritic stimulation.
source: Notably, compared to GCaMP6s, GCaMP6f had a reduced sensitivity for detecting calcium signals, specifically in the soma during low frequency spiking driven either by somatic or dendritic stimulation (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative ex vivo experimental data between the two calcium indicators.

claim: As compared to GCaMP6s, attenuation of events from soma to dendrite is underestimated with GCaMP6f.
source: Consequently, as compared to GCaMP6s, attenuation of events from soma to dendrite was underestimated whereas attenuation of events from dendrite to soma was overestimated with GCaMP6f (Figure 4G vs 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of the two calcium indicators shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: With GCaMP6s, attenuation of signals is asymmetric, with attenuation only found from soma to distal dendrites.
source: With GCaMP6s, by contrast, attenuation of signals was asymmetric; we only found attenuation from soma to distal dendrites, as observed in vivo (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data with GCaMP6s shown in Figure 4G.

claim: No global calcium signals are detected in the apical tuft when L1 stimulation fails to evoke a somatic action potential.
source: We could not detect any global calcium signals in the apical tuft when L1 stimulation failed to evoke a somatic action potential, indicating a strong coupling between global calcium events and somatic spiking in our experimental conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: When L1 stimulation only evokes a single action potential, apical tuft calcium signals are observed in 60% of the trials but are below the detection threshold of GCaMP6s in the soma.
source: When L1 stimulation only evoked a single action potential, apical tuft calcium signals were observed in 60% of the trials; however, these events were below the detection threshold of GCaMP6s in the soma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Provided L1 stimulation evokes at least two action potentials, calcium signals in both apical tuft and soma are robustly detected.
source: Provided L1 stimulation evoked at least two action potentials, calcium signals in both apical tuft and soma were robustly detected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Both somatic and dendritic calcium transients increase with the number of action potentials evoked by L1 stimulation.
source: Across stimulation parameters, both somatic and dendritic calcium transients increased with the number of action potentials evoked by L1 stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The relationship between calcium transient amplitude and percentage of attenuated events from soma to apical tuft remains unchanged by visual stimulation and behavioral-state changes.
source: These results indicate that the relationship between calcium transient amplitude and percentage of attenuated events from soma to apical tuft remained unchanged by visual stimulation and behavioural-state changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Three-way ANOVA) showing no significant effects of visual stimulation or locomotion.

claim: Neither visual stimulation nor locomotion alters the function relating calcium transient amplitude with the proportion of compartment-specific events (Three-way ANOVA, p=0.69, p=0.21 and p=0.64 for visual stimulation, locomotion, and interaction respectively).
source: We found that in all four conditions compartment-specific events were dominated by small amplitude calcium transients in proximal compartments: there was no significant difference between darkness and visual stimulation periods, both during stationary and locomotion periods (Figure 5B; Three-way ANOVA, p=0.69, p=0.21 and p=0.64 for visual stimulation, locomotion, and interaction respectively; p<10−15 for event amplitude; no other interaction was found to be statistically significant).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Three-way ANOVA) of calcium transients under different conditions.

claim: The percentage of coincident calcium signals across compartments of individual neurons is not significantly modified by visual stimulation or behavioral state changes.
source: In addition, we found that, on average, the percentage of coincident calcium signals across compartments of individual neurons was not significantly modified either by visual stimulation or behavioural state changes (n = 19 neurons) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The distribution of residual values across neuronal compartments is not significantly affected by locomotion or visual stimulation (Three-way ANOVA, p=0.96, p=0.23 and p=0.91 for visual stimulation, locomotion and interaction effect, respectively).
source: We found that the distribution of the residual values across neuronal compartments were neither significantly affected by locomotion nor by visual stimulation (Three-way ANOVA, p=0.96, p=0.23 and p=0.91 for visual stimulation, locomotion and interaction effect, respectively; p=0.86 for different compartments; no other interaction effect was found to be significant; n = 11 Soma–Trunk pairs; n = 5 pTrunk–dTrunk; n = 9 Trunk–Tuft; n = 6 pTuft-dTuft from 19 neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Three-way ANOVA) of residual values from robust linear regression.

claim: The selectivity of responses to drifting grating orientation does not affect the high correlation of calcium transients between tuft dendrites.
source: In the apical tuft, we found that the selectivity of the responses to the drifting gratings orientation, quantified by an orientation selectivity index (OSI), did not affect the high correlation of calcium transients between tuft dendrites (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of orientation selectivity and correlation values shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Locomotion similarly increases calcium transient amplitudes both in apical tuft and soma, without a significant difference between compartments (Paired t-test, p=0.38).
source: We found that locomotion similarly increased calcium transient amplitudes both in apical tuft and soma, without a significant difference between compartments (Figure 6G, Paired t-test, p=0.38), both during the presentation of preferred and non-preferred orientations (Figure 6H, Repeated measures Two-way ANOVA on log-transformed data, p=0.07, 0.71 and 0.28 for stimulus-type, compartment and interaction effects respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Paired t-test) of calcium transient amplitudes during locomotion.

claim: The orientation selectivity index (OSI) of somatic and apical tuft responses remains unchanged during both stationary and locomotion periods (Repeated measures Two-way ANOVA, p=0.49, p=0.42 and p=0.45, for the effects of locomotion, neuronal compartment and interaction, respectively).
source: As a consequence, the OSI of somatic and apical tuft responses remained unchanged during both stationary and locomotion periods (Figure 6I, Repeated measures Two-way ANOVA, p=0.49, p=0.42 and p=0.45, for the effects of locomotion, neuronal compartment and interaction, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Repeated measures Two-way ANOVA) of orientation selectivity indices.

claim: The preferred orientation is similar throughout tuft dendritic branches and neuronal compartments of individual neurons, both during stationary and locomotion periods.
source: In line with these results, we found that the preferred orientation was similar throughout tuft dendritic branches and neuronal compartments of individual neurons, both during stationary and locomotion periods (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of preferred orientations shown in Figure 6J and K.

claim: The Pearson's correlation between apical tuft branches calcium signals and across neuronal compartments remains high and unchanged regardless of the grating orientation.
source: Finally, the Pearson's correlation between apical tuft branches calcium signals and across neuronal compartments remained high and unchanged regardless of the gratings orientation (Figure 6L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6L and M.

claim: Active dendritic conductances impact the integration of synaptic inputs and the resulting somatic output.
source: Active dendritic conductances impact the integration of synaptic inputs and the resulting somatic output (Grienberger et al., 2015; Stuart and Spruston, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Different types of active dendritic currents support local dendritic nonlinear events, primarily driven by NMDA- and voltage-gated conductances.
source: Different types of active dendritic currents have been described to support local dendritic nonlinear events, primarily driven by NMDA- and voltage-gated conductances (Schiller et al., 1997; Larkum et al., 1999b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nonlinear dendritic spikes have been reported in the long apical dendrite and tuft of cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: In cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons, nonlinear dendritic spikes have been reported in the long apical dendrite and tuft, both in vitro and in vivo (Grienberger et al., 2015; Stuart and Spruston, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dendritic events in layer 5 neurons are generally associated with calcium influx both locally and globally in the apical tuft.
source: These dendritic events are generally associated with calcium influx both locally and globally in the apical tuft (Xu et al., 2012; Hill et al., 2013; Palmer et al., 2014; Cichon and Gan, 2015; Manita et al., 2015; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The coincident occurrence of back-propagating action potentials and tuft depolarization generates widespread calcium transients in the apical tuft dendrites.
source: Additionally, the coincident occurrence of back-propagating action potentials and tuft depolarization was shown to generate widespread calcium transients in the apical tuft dendrites (Spruston et al., 1995; Magee, 1997; Svoboda et al., 1997; Helmchen et al., 1999; Larkum et al., 1999b; Waters et al., 2003; Manita et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Events described as local dendritically-generated spikes were reported in layer 2/3 neurons of the visual and somatosensory cortex during sensory stimulation.
source: Events described as local dendritically-generated spikes were reported in layer 2/3 neurons of the visual and somatosensory cortex during sensory stimulation (Smith et al., 2013; Palmer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the visual cortex, it has been suggested that dendritic spikes triggered by visual input enhance somatic tuning to the preferred orientation.
source: In the visual cortex, it has been suggested that dendritic spikes triggered by visual input enhance somatic tuning to the preferred orientation (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: One study suggested that individual branches of densely labelled layer 5 neurons selectively display local calcium transients correlated with specific motor outputs.
source: Using calcium imaging in the mouse motor cortex, one study suggested that individual branches of densely labelled layer 5 neurons selectively display local calcium transients correlated with specific motor outputs (Cichon and Gan, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Other studies reported prevalent global calcium signals throughout layer 5 apical tuft dendrites in the barrel and motor cortex.
source: However, other studies reported prevalent global calcium signals throughout layer 5 apical tuft dendrites in the barrel and motor cortex (Xu et al., 2012; Hill et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Layer 5 apical dendritic calcium transients correlate with behaviourally relevant features.
source: While layer 5 apical dendritic calcium transients were shown to correlate with behaviourally relevant features (Xu et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2016; Peters et al., 2017; Ranganathan et al., 2018; Kerlin et al., 2019), the coupling between apical tuft activity and somatic output remains poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A recent study showed that apical trunk dendritic calcium signals were highly correlated with somatic signals in layer 5 neurons of the primary visual cortex (V1) of awake behaving mice.
source: By using semi-simultaneous imaging of apical trunk and somatic GCaMP6f signals in layer 5 neurons, a recent study has shown that apical trunk dendritic calcium signals were highly correlated with somatic signals in the primary visual cortex (V1) of awake behaving mice (Beaulieu-Laroche et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Layer 5 pyramidal neurons in V1 display selective responses to physical features of visual stimuli, such as the orientation and direction of movement.
source: Layer 5 pyramidal neurons in V1 display selective responses to physical features of visual stimuli, such as the orientation and direction of movement (Niell and Stryker, 2008; Kim et al., 2015) and their activity is modulated by locomotion (Erisken et al., 2014; Dadarlat and Stryker, 2017; Pakan et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Layer 5 neuron activity is modulated by locomotion.
source: Layer 5 pyramidal neurons in V1 display selective responses to physical features of visual stimuli, such as the orientation and direction of movement (Niell and Stryker, 2008; Kim et al., 2015) and their activity is modulated by locomotion (Erisken et al., 2014; Dadarlat and Stryker, 2017; Pakan et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Beaulieu-Laroche et al. (2019) found that neither visual stimulation nor locomotion altered the high somato-dendritic coupling of calcium transients.
source: However, Beaulieu-Laroche et al. (2019) found that neither visual stimulation nor locomotion altered the high somato-dendritic coupling of calcium transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dendritic signals attenuate in a distance-dependent manner.
source: Previous studies have shown that dendritic signals attenuate in a distance-dependent manner, suggesting that at least some of the calcium events generated in one compartment would attenuate as they reach the next compartment (Stuart et al., 1997; Svoboda et al., 1997; Helmchen et al., 1999; Vetter et al., 2001; Larkum et al., 2009; Waters et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At least 40% of somatic calcium transients are not triggered by apical tuft calcium events.
source: These results indicate that at least 40% of somatic calcium transients were not triggered by apical tuft calcium events, and that these transients attenuated from the soma to the apical tuft.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the measured proportions of attenuated events in different directions.

claim: Attenuated calcium transients are associated with low-frequency back-propagating somatic action potentials, below the critical frequency required to trigger dendritic electrogenesis.
source: Based on our ex vivo recordings, we suggest that attenuated calcium transients are associated with low-frequency back-propagating somatic action potentials, below the critical frequency required to trigger dendritic electrogenesis (Larkum et al., 1999a; Shai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ex vivo experimental data and is supported by citations to previous literature on dendritic electrogenesis.

claim: Attenuation may involve active inhibitory mechanisms along the somato-dendritic axis.
source: Attenuation may also involve active inhibitory mechanisms along the somato-dendritic axis (Larkum et al., 1999a; Naka and Adesnik, 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A recent study reported that 83.9% (median) of dendritic calcium signal (rise events) were paired with events in the soma while 73.4% of somatic events were paired with dendritic ones.
source: A recent study reported a high and symmetric somato-dendritic coupling in V1 layer 5 neurons concluding that GCaMP6f events occurred concurrently in soma and dendritic compartments (Beaulieu-Laroche et al., 2019). The authors reported that 83.9% (median) of dendritic calcium signal (rise events) were paired with events in the soma while 73.4% of somatic events were paired with dendritic ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In this study, 98.6% of dendritic events were paired with somatic ones and 60% of somatic events were paired with dendritic ones.
source: In our study, we found a stronger asymmetry with 98.6% of dendritic events paired with somatic ones and 60 % of somatic events paired with dendritic ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from this study.

claim: The discrepancy between this study and Beaulieu-Laroche et al. (2019) may be explained by differences in imaging conditions including denser labelling and the use of GCaMP6f.
source: This discrepancy may be explained by differences in imaging conditions including a denser labelling, which increases the amount of background signals, and the use of GCaMP6f, which has a lower signal amplitude and signal-to-noise ratio than the GCaMP6s indicator used in our study, leading to a lower probability of detecting small events in layer 5 somata, as shown by our ex vivo recordings (Figure 4G-H).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from methodological differences and ex vivo experimental data.

claim: High somato-dendritic coupling occurs during either high frequency back propagating action potentials or strong apical tuft activity capable of driving somatic spiking.
source: Based on our ex vivo experiments, high somato-dendritic coupling would occur during either 1) high frequency back propagating action potentials or 2) strong apical tuft activity capable of driving somatic spiking.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ex vivo experimental data.

claim: Coupling could occur with lower frequency back propagating action potentials, provided they are paired with tuft inputs.
source: Coupling could in principle also be observed with lower frequency back propagating action potentials, provided they are paired with tuft inputs (Larkum, 2013; Manita et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Apical tuft signals and somato-dendritic coupling may differ between different subtypes of layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Notably, both apical tuft signals and the somato-dendritic coupling may differ between different subtypes of layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on known differences between layer 5 neuron subtypes.

claim: At least two main types of layer 5 pyramidal neurons exist: intratelencephalic neurons which connect cortical areas, and pyramidal tract neurons which project to multiple subcortical areas.
source: It is known that at least two main types exist: intratelencephalic neurons which connect cortical areas, and pyramidal tract neurons which project to multiple subcortical areas (Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Gerfen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The two types of layer 5 pyramidal neurons display different morphologies and receive different types of inputs.
source: These two types display different morphologies (Groh et al., 2010) and receive different types of inputs (Young, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The neurons included in this study mainly displayed thick-tufted morphology, characteristic of pyramidal tract neurons.
source: The neurons included in this study had their soma located at various depths within layer 5 (median 528 μm, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and mainly displayed thick-tufted morphology, characteristic of pyramidal tract neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis of the imaged neurons.

claim: The prevalence and dynamics of synaptic inputs received by layer 5 pyramidal neurons strongly vary between passive sensory stimulation and active learning tasks.
source: It is known that the prevalence and the dynamics of synaptic inputs received by layer 5 pyramidal neurons strongly vary between passive sensory stimulation and active learning tasks (Xu et al., 2012; Hong et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Apical tuft dendrites of layer 5 neurons receive a barrage of thousands of synaptic inputs in vivo.
source: Apical tuft dendrites of layer 5 neurons receive a barrage of thousands of synaptic inputs in vivo (Stuart and Spruston, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: V1 neurons receive synaptic inputs conveying information not only about visual stimuli but also about non-visual variables (e.g. arousal/attention, motor activity, reward-related and spatial information).
source: it was shown that V1 neurons receive synaptic inputs conveying information not only about visual stimuli but also about non-visual variables (e.g. arousal/attention, motor activity, reward-related and spatial information) (Pakan et al., 2016; Pakan et al., 2018a; Pakan et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both inhibitory and neuromodulatory inputs modulate electrical interactions between soma and dendrites in layer 5 neurons.

source: It is therefore possible that during the active learning of a behavioural task, the synaptic inputs associated with this learning process would lead to different mechanisms of dendritic integration than during passive viewing.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature and ex vivo experimental data from this study.

claim: Branch-specific stimulation can trigger localized Ca2+ events detected by calcium indicators ex vivo.
source: Whereas ex vivo studies have demonstrated that branch-specific stimulation can trigger localized Ca2+ events detected by calcium indicators (e.g. Cai et al., 2004; Sandler et al., 2016; review: Major et al., 2013), the detection of these events in vivo is more challenging, principally because they may be masked by ongoing global dendritic events (Kerlin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lowering the detection threshold by 30% in one of two paired branches reduced the proportion of branch-specific events from 3.8% to 0.8%.
source: We found that lowering the threshold by 30% in one of the two pair branches reduced the proportion of branch-specific events from 3.8% to 0.8%, suggesting that most of these already rare events were near detection threshold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of detection threshold effects shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Action potentials evoked by dendritic stimulation were accompanied by an enhanced afterdepolarization in the soma, characteristic of distal dendritic electrogenesis.

claim: The critical frequency of back-propagating action potentials required to trigger distal dendritic calcium spikes is 50–100 Hz.
source: By contrast, in the distal dendrites, reliable signals for both indicators were only detected when somatically-driven spiking exceeded 50 Hz (Figure 4E–H), likely reflecting the critical frequency (50–100 Hz) of back-propagating action potentials required to trigger distal dendritic calcium spikes (Larkum et al., 1999a; Shai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Evoked apical tuft calcium events are strongly coupled to somatic spiking.
source: Collectively, our findings reveal that evoked apical tuft calcium events are strongly coupled to somatic spiking, and that this coupling can be detected by GCaMP6s imaging provided that somatic output is above the limits of detection (≥2 action potentials ex vivo).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo experimental data.

claim: Around 40% of somatic calcium transients decay by the time they reach the apical tuft.
source: Our results show that while around 40% of somatic calcium transients decay by the time they reach the apical tuft, only 1.4% of apical tuft calcium events were not associated with somatic events (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium transient attenuation.
